ev.q: Vascular access via central venous catheter was strongly associated with S. aureus bloodstream infections
Adjusting for EIP site of residence, sex, and vascular access type, S. aureus bloodstream infection risk in EIP was highest in Hispanic patients
the S. aureus bloodstream infection rate during 2017–2020 was 100 times higher among hemodialysis patients (4,248 of 100,000 person-years)
42.1% of S. aureus bloodstream infections among patients on hemodialysis occurred in tracts in the highest quartile
S. aureus was isolated from 5,070 (34.2%), yielding a rate of 0.1 S. aureus bloodstream infections per 100 patient-months
Unadjusted rates of S. aureus bloodstream infection were higher among Black and Hispanic hemodialysis patients
Multivariable analyses demonstrated that Hispanic ethnicity (aRR = 1.4; 95% CI = 1.2–1.7)
Surveillance data from the 2020 National Healthcare Safety Network (NHSN) and the 2017–2020 Emerging Infections Program (EIP) were used
analyses of 2020 NHSN facility–reported bloodstream infection data relied on linkage with ecologic 2018 SVI data
this study used a national facility-level reporting system and a laboratory- and population-based surveillance network

methods_quotes.q: To handle overdispersion, negative binomial regression was performed to determine aRRs for age, race and ethnicity, sex, vascular access type, and EIP site.
Incidences for S. aureus bloodstream infections were created by pooling events as the numerator and patient-months as the denominator
S. aureus bloodstream infection incidence was modeled using forward stage-wise negative binomial regression.
U.S. Census Bureau tracts under surveillance were grouped by quartile for each measure of SES factors
